title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 5.2.1 Reading: Extensive Reading

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Extensive reading means reading widely on your own, for meaning and for pleasure. In this sub-strand you will choose stories, poems and simple articles that suit your age, practise ways to read more smoothly, and retell what you have read about food and health.

## Strand 5.0: Nutrition - Balanced Diet
Sub-strand 5.2.1: Reading: Extensive Reading
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) select appropriate reading materials for lifelong learning
b) read a variety of familiar materials independently to build reading speed and fluency
c) apply appropriate strategies to read independently for information and enjoyment
d) realise the importance of independent reading in lifelong learning

## What this sub-strand covers
• Independent Reading

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should we read widely?
2. What materials do you enjoy reading?

## Core competencies
• Digital Literacy: This is developed as the learner uses selected reading materials from electronic sources.
• Learning to Learn: It is enhanced as the learner develops extensive reading strategies in their language clubs.

## Values
• Responsibility: This is cultivated as the learner engages diligently in assigned tasks on independent.
• Love: This is enhanced as the learner respects other learners' opinions when reading.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Life skills : Effective communication is demonstrated as the learner reads a variety of materials to build speed and fluency.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to link the concept of independent reading to Kiswahili.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 5.0 Nutrition – Balanced Diet, Sub-strand 5.2.1 Extensive Reading

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Choosing what to read

LESSON 1: CHOOSING WHAT TO READ
===============================

## What you will learn
• Choose a text that is interesting and mostly readable at Grade 4.
• Tell a narrative, a poem, a magazine and a newspaper page apart.
• Explain why reading many kinds of texts helps learning later in life.

Curriculum outcomes: a) select appropriate reading materials for lifelong learning; d) realise the importance of independent reading in lifelong learning

## Introduction
A thick book full of words you cannot say is not a brave choice. It is a frustrating one. A good independent book is interesting, mostly clear, and still gives you a few new words to keep.

## Notes
### What to look for
Age-appropriate means the ideas and the words fit a learner of about nine or ten. High-interest means you actually want to know what happens. Both matter. A book can be suitable and still bore you, or exciting and still too hard.

Try this test. Read one page. If you miss only a few words and you still understand the page, the text is in a good range. If almost every line stops you, choose another text and ask your teacher for a next step, rather than pretending.

### Kinds of texts
- A narrative tells a story, with people, a place and events in order.
- A poem uses short lines, rhythm and sometimes rhyme. It can be read aloud more than once.
- A magazine often mixes short articles, pictures and interviews. A children's page is a good start.
- A newspaper reports events. Some articles are hard. Begin with a short item that has a picture and a headline you understand.

You can find these on paper or on a screen. Electronic texts are fine when a teacher or parent has opened them for you. A random link is not a library. Stay with the book, poem or site an adult has approved.

### A reason to read widely
One story can show a character choosing fruit. A poem can make you hear the words. A short article can tell you why water matters. Together they build a habit of finding things out without waiting for a lesson. That habit is part of lifelong learning: you will still need to read instructions, stories and news when nobody is marking your book.

Ask yourself three questions before you borrow a text. Do I understand most of it? Do I want to finish it? Is an adult happy for me to read it? If you can say yes, take it.

## Key words
• extensive reading — reading many texts on your own for meaning, fluency and enjoyment
• age-appropriate — suitable for your age in words and ideas
• narrative — a text that tells a story
• headline — the title in large print at the top of a news item

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You miss about four words on a page but you understand the story. Is the book a reasonable choice?

Working:
1. The test allows a few new words.
2. You still understand the page, and you can ask about those words later.

Answer: Yes. It is challenging enough without being too hard.

### Example 2
Sort these into narrative, poem or newspaper: a piece with short rhyming lines about mangoes; a story about a market; a report with a headline about a school garden.

Working:
1. Rhyming lines are a poem.
2. Events about people at a market make a narrative.
3. A headline and a report belong to a newspaper.

Answer: Poem; narrative; newspaper.

## Activity: Build a reading choice
You will need: A small pile of class readers, poems, a children's magazine or newspaper page, A device only if the teacher opens an approved text
1. Look through three texts. Read the title and one short part of each.
2. Choose one you can mostly read and that you want to finish.
3. Tell a partner the title, the kind of text, and one reason you chose it.
4. Agree where an after-school reading club could meet, and what rule you will follow about approved websites.

## Practice
1. What does age-appropriate mean?
2. Name two kinds of texts you can read independently.
3. Why is a random link not the same as a library book?

## Summary
• Choose texts you mostly understand and truly want to read.
• Narratives, poems, magazines and newspapers give different kinds of reading.
• Wide reading is a habit you can keep after school.

### Answers to practice
1. The words and ideas suit a learner of your age.
2. Any two of: narratives, poems, magazines, newspapers, approved electronic texts.
3. A teacher or parent has not checked it. Stay with texts an adult has approved.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Ways to read on your own

LESSON 2: WAYS TO READ ON YOUR OWN
==================================

## What you will learn
• Use previewing, silent reading and re-reading to understand a text.
• Keep a simple reading log.
• Read a familiar passage more smoothly the second time.

Curriculum outcomes: b) read a variety of familiar materials independently to build reading speed and fluency; c) apply appropriate strategies to read independently for information and enjoyment

## Introduction
Reading speed is not a race to skip words. Fluency means you recognise words quickly enough to keep the meaning. A few steady strategies will take you further than rushing.

## Notes
### Before you read
Look at the title, the pictures and any words in bold. Ask, 'What do I think this is about?' This preview gives your mind a place to put the details.

### While you read
Read silently. Your lips do not have to move. Follow the sentences, not one lonely word at a time. When a sentence is smooth, your eyes can take in a short group of words, such as 'the ripe mangoes' or 'on the wooden table'.

If a new word appears, finish the sentence. Sometimes the next words explain it. If the meaning is still missing, underline the word or write it down and keep going, as long as you still know what is happening. Stop and ask only when the whole paragraph has become unclear.

### After a bumpy paragraph
Re-read that paragraph once, more slowly. Repeated reading of a short, familiar text is one of the best ways to become fluent. The second reading should sound calmer if you read it aloud to a partner.

### A log worth keeping
A reading log is a few lines, not a project.

- Date
- Title and kind of text
- One sentence about what happened or what you learnt
- One new word and a meaning in your own words

Ten quiet minutes a day will do more than one long session you never repeat. Use classroom readers, library books and texts your teacher has placed on a tablet. Record pleasure honestly: you are allowed to say which part you enjoyed and which part was confusing.

### Two warnings
Do not move your finger under every letter if you already know the words. The finger can slow you down. Do use it for a line you find hard, then lift it again.

Do not copy a whole page into your log. A log helps you remember. It is not a second book.

## Key words
• fluency — reading words accurately and smoothly enough to follow the meaning
• preview — a quick look at the title and pictures before you read the whole text
• reading log — a short record of what you read, when you read it, and one thing you learnt
• re-read — to read a part again so the meaning and the sound become clearer

## Worked examples

### Example 1
You do not know the word 'deficiency', but the next sentence says 'a lack of something the body needs'. What should you do?

Working:
1. Finish the sentence that explains the word.
2. Note the meaning, then continue.

Answer: Take the meaning from the next sentence, write the word in your log if you wish, and read on.

### Example 2
A learner's log says only 'I read'. What should be added?

Working:
1. A log needs the date, the title, one fact or event, and perhaps a new word.

Answer: The date, the title, one sentence about the text, and one new word with its meaning.

## Activity: Silent reading and a log
You will need: A familiar class reader or the story in the next lesson, A reading-log page
1. Preview the title and any picture for half a minute.
2. Read silently for several minutes. Mark one new word without stopping for long.
3. Re-read one paragraph aloud to a partner, more smoothly than the first time.
4. Fill four lines of a reading log: date, title, one sentence, one new word.

## Practice
1. What do you look at during a preview?
2. Why do you re-read a bumpy paragraph?
3. Name the four lines of a simple reading log.

## Summary
• Preview, read silently, and re-read parts that were unclear.
• Fluency grows when you read a text more than once.
• A short log helps you remember without copying the book.

### Answers to practice
1. The title, the pictures and any bold words, then you ask what the text might be about.
2. The second reading makes the meaning clearer and helps you say the words more smoothly.
3. Date, title, one sentence about the text, and one new word with its meaning.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Read, retell and give an opinion

LESSON 3: READ, RETELL AND GIVE AN OPINION
==========================================

## What you will learn
• Read a short narrative independently and retell it in order.
• Share an opinion and listen to a different opinion with respect.
• Use a reading strategy while you read.

Curriculum outcomes: b) read a variety of familiar materials independently to build reading speed and fluency; c) apply appropriate strategies to read independently for information and enjoyment; d) realise the importance of independent reading in lifelong learning

## Introduction
Retelling is the proof that you read. If the events come out in a muddle, the remedy is not a longer speech. It is another quiet look at the story.

## Notes
### Market Morning
Read this narrative silently. It is written for you to manage alone.

Achieng woke early because her aunt was going to the market. She packed a bottle of drinking water and a small coin purse. At the first stall, pyramids of mangoes glowed in the sun. Next to them, a trader shook a basin of beans. 'Protein,' Achieng whispered, proud of the word from class.

Her aunt bought maize flour, the beans, a bunch of sukuma wiki and four oranges. Achieng pointed at a tall pile of sweets. 'Those are only sugar,' her aunt said gently. 'We can share one orange on the way home. The rest of the food will make a real meal.'

On the path they met a neighbour carrying a tiny baby. The aunt added an extra orange to the neighbour's bag. 'Young children need meals that suit them,' she said. 'If a child is very weak, we tell the clinic. We do not decide the illness on the road.'

At home, Achieng washed her hands, drank some water and helped sort the beans. She wrote one sentence in her reading log, then laughed, because the log was about her own morning, not about a book. 'I would still like a story tonight,' she said. Her aunt opened a thin storybook. They read it side by side.

### Retell without copying every line
A retelling needs the bones of the story.

1. Achieng went to the market with her aunt.
2. They bought maize flour, beans, sukuma wiki and oranges, and they left the pile of sweets.
3. The aunt gave an orange to a neighbour and said a weak child should be taken to a clinic, not diagnosed on the road.
4. At home they prepared food, and later they read a book together.

### Opinions
An opinion is what you think. 'I liked the aunt's kindness' is an opinion. 'They bought beans' is a fact. Both are welcome. If a partner liked the market scene more than the ending, listen. You do not have to change your mind, and you do not have to win. Say, 'I see it differently because...' and stop there.

Independent reading matters because nobody can sit beside you for every page of your life. Each book you finish makes the next one a little easier.

## Key words
• retell — to give the main events again in order, in your own words
• opinion — what you think or feel about a text, which others may not share
• fact — something the text states, which you can point to

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Is this a fact or an opinion: 'The aunt bought beans'?

Working:
1. Check the story.
2. The sentence reports an event that happened in the narrative.

Answer: A fact

### Example 2
Give one opinion about Market Morning and one reason.

Working:
1. Choose a feeling or a judgement.
2. Tie it to an event so it is more than 'it was nice'.

Answer: I think the aunt was wise because she chose food for a meal and refused a tall pile of sweets.

## Activity: Reading club circle
You will need: Market Morning or another familiar story, Reading logs
1. Read the story silently. Use a preview and mark one new word.
2. In a circle, retell the story together, each person adding the next event.
3. Each learner shares one opinion. The next learner says what they heard before giving a different view.
4. Write a log entry. Agree to meet again as an after-school club and bring a different text next time.

## Practice
1. What four foods did the aunt buy?
2. Why did the aunt refuse the tall pile of sweets?
3. What is the difference between a fact and an opinion in a retelling?
4. Why does independent reading matter after you leave class?

## Summary
• Retell the main events in order and in your own words.
• Label facts and opinions differently, and respect both.
• Independent reading is a habit that outlasts one lesson.

### Answers to practice
1. Maize flour, beans, sukuma wiki and oranges.
2. They are only sugar. She wanted food that would make a real meal, and they could share an orange instead.
3. A fact is an event or detail from the text. An opinion is what you think about it.
4. You will still need to read stories, instructions and news when a teacher is not beside you. Each text you finish makes the next one easier.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 5.2.1 READING: EXTENSIVE READING
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. A text is a good independent choice when
   A. you know none of the words
   B. you understand most of a page and you want to read it
   C. it has no title
   D. a stranger sent the link

2. Short lines and rhyme usually tell you the text is
   A. a poem
   B. a number plate
   C. a shopping list
   D. an address

3. Why should you avoid a random internet link for reading practice?
   A. Screens cannot show words
   B. An adult has not approved it
   C. Poems are illegal
   D. Newspapers have no headlines

4. A preview means
   A. copying the whole text
   B. looking at the title and pictures before you read
   C. closing the book
   D. skipping the ending

5. Re-reading a short passage helps fluency because
   A. the words become more familiar and the meaning clearer
   B. you must add new events
   C. you should never read silently
   D. the title changes

6. A reading log should include
   A. the whole story copied out
   B. the date, the title, one sentence and a new word
   C. only a drawing of a sweet
   D. another learner's password

7. In Market Morning the aunt said a very weak child should
   A. be given a nickname
   B. be taken to a clinic, not diagnosed on the road
   C. eat only sweets
   D. stay away from water

8. 'I liked the ending' is
   A. a fact about the price of beans
   B. an opinion
   C. a headline
   D. a vitamin

9. Why is wide reading useful for lifelong learning?
   A. You will never need to read again
   B. You practise finding meaning in stories, poems and information on your own
   C. It replaces drinking water
   D. It removes every new word from English

10. Retell one event from Market Morning in a sentence.
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 5.2.1 READING: EXTENSIVE READING
========================================

1. B. you understand most of a page and you want to read it
   Interest and a comfortable number of known words make a text suitable.

2. A. a poem
   Poems are often set in short lines and may rhyme.

3. B. An adult has not approved it
   Use print or electronic texts that a teacher or parent has approved.

4. B. looking at the title and pictures before you read
   Previewing prepares you for the meaning.

5. A. the words become more familiar and the meaning clearer
   Repeated reading of a familiar text builds smooth, accurate reading.

6. B. the date, the title, one sentence and a new word
   A log is a short record, not a copy of the book.

7. B. be taken to a clinic, not diagnosed on the road
   She refused to decide an illness herself.

8. B. an opinion
   It says what the reader thinks, which another reader may not share.

9. B. You practise finding meaning in stories, poems and information on your own
   Independent reading is a habit that continues outside class.

10. Achieng and her aunt bought maize flour, beans, sukuma wiki and oranges, and they did not buy the pile of sweets.
   A retelling gives a main event in the reader's own words.

Independent reading matters because nobody can sit beside you for every page of your life. Each book you finish makes the next one a little easier.

## Key words
• retell — to give the main events again in order, in your own words
• opinion — what you think or feel about a text, which others may not share
• fact — something the text states, which you can point to

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Is this a fact or an opinion: 'The aunt bought beans'?

Working:
1. Check the story.
2. The sentence reports an event that happened in the narrative.

Answer: A fact

### Example 2
Give one opinion about Market Morning and one reason.

Working:
1. Choose a feeling or a judgement.
2. Tie it to an event so it is more than 'it was nice'.

Answer: I think the aunt was wise because she chose food for a meal and refused a tall pile of sweets.

## Activity: Reading club circle
You will need: Market Morning or another familiar story, Reading logs
1. Read the story silently. Use a preview and mark one new word.
2. In a circle, retell the story together, each person adding the next event.
3. Each learner shares one opinion. The next learner says what they heard before giving a different view.
4. Write a log entry. Agree to meet again as an after-school club and bring a different text next time.

## Practice
1. What four foods did the aunt buy?
2. Why did the aunt refuse the tall pile of sweets?
3. What is the difference between a fact and an opinion in a retelling?
4. Why does independent reading matter after you leave class?

## Summary
• Retell the main events in order and in your own words.
• Label facts and opinions differently, and respect both.
• Independent reading is a habit that outlasts one lesson.

### Answers to practice
1. Maize flour, beans, sukuma wiki and oranges.
2. They are only sugar. She wanted food that would make a real meal, and they could share an orange instead.
3. A fact is an event or detail from the text. An opinion is what you think about it.
4. You will still need to read stories, instructions and news when a teacher is not beside you. Each text you finish makes the next one easier.

questions.question: A text is a good independent choice when
options: you know none of the words
you understand most of a page and you want to read it
questions.explanation: Interest and a comfortable number of known words make a text suitable.

questions.question: Short lines and rhyme usually tell you the text is
questions.explanation: Poems are often set in short lines and may rhyme.

questions.question: Why should you avoid a random internet link for reading practice?
options: An adult has not approved it
questions.explanation: Use print or electronic texts that a teacher or parent has approved.

questions.question: A preview means
options: looking at the title and pictures before you read
questions.explanation: Previewing prepares you for the meaning.

questions.question: Re-reading a short passage helps fluency because
options: the words become more familiar and the meaning clearer
questions.explanation: Repeated reading of a familiar text builds smooth, accurate reading.

questions.question: A reading log should include
options: the date, the title, one sentence and a new word
only a drawing of a sweet
questions.explanation: A log is a short record, not a copy of the book.

questions.question: In Market Morning the aunt said a very weak child should
options: be taken to a clinic, not diagnosed on the road
questions.explanation: She refused to decide an illness herself.

questions.question: 'I liked the ending' is
options: a fact about the price of beans
questions.explanation: It says what the reader thinks, which another reader may not share.

questions.question: Why is wide reading useful for lifelong learning?
options: You will never need to read again
You practise finding meaning in stories, poems and information on your own
It removes every new word from English
questions.explanation: Independent reading is a habit that continues outside class.

questions.question: Retell one event from Market Morning in a sentence.
questions.answer: Achieng and her aunt bought maize flour, beans, sukuma wiki and oranges, and they did not buy the pile of sweets.
questions.explanation: A retelling gives a main event in the reader's own words.
